Q25409451.summary: Bishop Marianos of Faras stands in rich vestments, a book in his hand, beside the Virgin, who holds the Christ Child on her left arm. A full-length figure of the adult Christ originally stood at the bishop's side and laid his hand on Marianos's shoulder, but only fragments of it survive. Painted when Marianos took office, the image placed the Nubian bishop under the protection of Christ and his Mother.
facts: Marianos was bishop of Faras from 1005 to 1036; the painting is one of fourteen bishop portraits found in Faras Cathedral.
It was discovered by Polish archaeologists during the UNESCO-sponsored Nubian campaign of the 1960s and has been in the National Museum in Warsaw since 1964.
Of the adult Christ, only the nimbus, part of the leg and garment, and the fingers resting on the bishop's shoulder remain.

links.label: Wikipedia (pl): Biskup Marianos pod opieką Chrystusa i Matki Boskiej

Q25409451.notes: Wikidata labels the style 'Coptic art'; it is Nubian (Makurian) painting. The Christ Child is clearly visible; the adult Christ survives only in fragments.

commons:8915912.summary: Against a gold ground, the Virgin holds the infant Christ while Joseph stands close beside her, and a priest stretches out his hands to them before a domed sanctuary at the right; a mountain with trees rises at the left. The miniature marks the feast of Christ's Circumcision on the first of January, when the Child received the name Jesus. Its graceful figures and modelled landscape show the classicising refinement of Constantinople's court painters around the year 1000.
facts: The Menologion of Basil II, made in Constantinople for Emperor Basil II (r. 976–1025), contains some 430 miniatures and covers only the half of the church year from September to February.
Unusually, the names of eight painters, including Pantoleon, are written beside the miniatures, though all in the same scribe's hand.
The manuscript was owned in the 15th century by Ludovico Sforza, Duke of Milan, and given to Pope Paul V in the early 17th century; it is now Vat. gr. 1613.
commons:8915912.notes: The Commons description places this miniature on f. 287 and gives an 11th-century date; Wikipedia dates the manuscript c. 1000 (between 979 and the early 11th century). The painter's name for this miniature was not checked.

commons:201904405.summary: A youthful shepherd with a cap of curls stands on a small base, carrying a ram across his shoulders and steadying its legs with his right hand. He wears a belted short tunic and leggings, and a further animal lies at his feet; a supporting pillar rises behind him, and his left forearm is broken away. Small statuettes like this one turned the familiar pastoral figure into an image of Christ, who lays down his life for his sheep.
facts: The Museum of Byzantine Culture labels the statuette 'The Good Shepherd' and dates it to the 4th century (a photograph of the label reads 'second decade of the 4th century'; another source says mid-4th century).
Freestanding Good Shepherd statuettes are among the earliest Christian sculptures in the round; the type adapts the classical calf- or ram-bearer (kriophoros).

links.label: Wikimedia Commons: Statuette of the Good Shepherd, Museum of Byzantine Culture

commons:201904405.notes: Precise dating within the 4th century differs between sources. Medium (marble) is identified from photographs. As with all early Good Shepherd statuettes, the Christian reading rests on context and the museum's identification.

cur:catacombs-cordoba-sarcophagus.summary: Columns divide the front into niches with Old and New Testament scenes – among them the Fall of Adam and Eve and Moses striking the rock – and the deceased, alongside scenes of Christ. Found in Córdoba itself, it is one of the finest early Christian sarcophagi in Spain.
facts: The museum dates it to the first third of the 4th century and records that it was found in the city of Córdoba.
Commons has detailed photographs of its Original Sin and Moses scenes.
cur:catacombs-cordoba-sarcophagus.notes: The Christ scenes were not individually verified.

cur:objects-lorsch-gospels-front-cover-v.summary: Five ivory panels form one of the grandest Carolingian book covers: at the top two angels hold a medallion with the bust of Christ blessing; in the centre the Virgin sits enthroned with the Christ Child, between St John the Baptist and the prophet Zacharias; and at the bottom are the Nativity and the Annunciation to the Shepherds. Classical architecture and drapery show how deliberately Charlemagne's artists revived the art of Late Antiquity. The cover proclaims the Incarnation: the eternal Son, blessing from heaven, born of the Virgin.
facts: The V&A explains that the panels formed the front cover of the Lorsch Gospels, a Gospel book of about 810 listed in the Lorsch abbey library catalogue of about 860; the back cover, with Christ treading on the beasts, is in the Museo Sacro of the Vatican.
The manuscript was taken to Heidelberg in 1556 with the Bibliotheca Palatina and divided; its first volume is now in Alba Iulia (Batthyaneum) and the second in the Vatican.
In 2023 UNESCO inscribed the whole group of ivories and manuscripts in its Memory of the World register.
cur:objects-lorsch-gospels-front-cover-v.notes: Companion of the existing featured entry 'lorsch-gospels-ivory-christ-treading-beasts' (Vatican back cover); this is a separate object.

cur:objects2-seal-peter-i-irene.summary: On the obverse of this small lead seal Christ appears as Pantokrator, a frontal half-length bust with cross-nimbus; on the reverse Tsar Peter I of Bulgaria and his Byzantine wife Irene (Maria) Lekapene stand side by side, holding a patriarchal cross between them. The arrangement copies the imperial seals and coins of Constantinople, where Christ occupies the place of honour above the rulers who govern in his name.
facts: Irene (Maria) Lekapene was a granddaughter of Emperor Romanos I Lekapenos; her marriage to Peter in 927 sealed peace between Byzantium and Bulgaria.
The design of a ruling couple holding a cross between them follows contemporary Byzantine imperial iconography.
cur:objects2-seal-peter-i-irene.notes: Numismatic-trade specimen photographed by CNG; one entry stands for the seal type.

walters:54.2666.summary: This small, oval bronze pendant has a loop for hanging. On one side, roughly incised, a haloed figure in a long robe stands against a cross with arms outstretched, which the Walters identifies as Christ crucified. On the other, a rider on horseback spears a figure lying beneath the horse, framed by an inscription band. Worn on the body, the pairing of the holy horseman with the Crucifixion called on Christ's victory for the wearer's protection.
facts: The pendant is only about 5 × 2.3 cm; the Walters bought it from Simon Bendall, London, in 1991.
walters:54.2666.notes: Date 5th–6th century per the museum (its CSV begin-year '-499' is an error). The incised Crucifixion is very schematic; the robe and halo are visible but no inscription can be read in the photographs.

walters:45.15.summary: This small gold ring has an octagonal hoop, each facet engraved and inlaid with black niello with a scene from the life of Christ. On the oval bezel the Ascension is shown in two registers: above, Christ sits in a mandorla carried up by angels, while below the Virgin stands among the apostles, who look up. Worn on the hand, the ring formed what the Walters calls 'a prayer in pictures'.
facts: The Walters notes that the ring's eight Gospel scenes were thought to have protective power, together forming a prayer in pictures.
An inscription around it quotes Isaiah 6:3, the angels' hymn: 'Holy, holy, holy is the Lord of Hosts'.
walters:45.15.notes: Date 6th–7th century per the Walters (Commons gives 6th century).

walters:W.44.97R.summary: The initial S of 'Salvum me fac, Deus' ('Save me, O God, for the waters have come in even unto my soul') is split into two scenes: below, the crowned King David stands naked to the waist in green water, arms flung upward; above, the haloed Christ leans down from the curve of the letter, holding a scroll and gesturing toward him. The image turns the psalmist's cry into a direct encounter between the drowning king and his Saviour.
facts: Psalm 68 ('Salvum me fac') is one of the ten divisions of this Psalter (Psalms 1, 26, 38, 51, 52, 68, 80, 97, 101 and 109), each marked by a historiated initial.
This is one of the ten historiated initials original to the Psalter, made c. 1250–1275 in French Flanders.
The Walters records that fourteenth-century additions were made for the use of a woman, showing the book stayed in female hands.

links.label: The Digital Walters: Psalter for a Cistercian woman (W.44)

walters:W.44.97R.notes: Worklist year 750 was a parsing error for '3rd quarter 13th century'.

Q19607289.summary: Rarely has a sacred subject been painted with such domestic tenderness: the boy Jesus, newly found in the Temple, stands with arms folded, while Mary, seated with an open book, gently reproaches him and Joseph gestures as if to explain. The jewel-like colours and gold ground are pure Sienese Gothic, yet the emotion is utterly human. Simone painted it at the papal court in Avignon, where he spent his last years.
facts: The panel is signed and dated 1342, one of Simone's last works; he died in Avignon in 1344.
The book Mary holds is inscribed with her words from Luke: 'Son, why hast thou thus dealt with us?'
The subject — the family's reunion after the search, rather than Jesus disputing with the doctors — is very rare in medieval art.
